assessment.nobel_worthiness: Time-reversal-invariant topological insulators and the quantum spin Hall effect opened a new class of quantum matter in which band topology, spin-orbit coupling and protected edge or surface states determine measurable behaviour. The theory is clear and general, it was tested against real band structures, and it reshaped how we search for materials. This is the kind of discovery where quantum mechanics surprises us in solids and where first-principles electronic structure became predictive.
assessment.attribution: Kane and Mele introduced the Z2 classification and the quantum spin Hall proposal for graphene. Molenkamp's group gave the decisive experimental demonstration in HgTe quantum wells, following the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang prediction. That prediction, and the 3D topological insulator work by Fu, Kane, Mele, Moore, Balents and Hasan, sit partly outside the credited names, so the three-person configuration is defensible but not unique. I choose theory plus decisive experiment from the supplied credit.
assessment.maturity: More than fifteen years of independent confirmation across HgTe, Bi-based compounds and ARPES, with a stable interpretation and a large follow-on literature. Recognition is timely and arguably overdue.
uncertainties: Credit for the HgTe quantum well prediction (Bernevig, Hughes, Zhang) is not in the supplied credited names.
Boundary with the 3D topological insulator discovery and with candidate B050 is unresolved.
I have not independently verified priority details from memory.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Dynamical mean-field theory is the first controlled, quantitative framework for strongly correlated electrons that captures both the Mott transition and coherent quasiparticles. Combined with DFT (DFT+DMFT) it makes quantitative predictions of spectra and phase behaviour in real materials. It is a conceptual and methodological advance with lasting impact, and it connects directly to the spectroscopy I care about.
assessment.attribution: Metzner and Vollhardt showed the infinite-dimension limit, Georges and Kotliar derived the mapping onto an impurity model, and Kotliar and collaborators built the material-specific DFT+DMFT. The three credited names cover the core, though Metzner, Müller-Hartmann and Jarrell are important and not credited. The allocation is reasonable but contestable.
assessment.maturity: More than thirty years of use and testing against photoemission and optical data, with independent codes in wide use. Limits (momentum dependence, cluster extensions, double counting in DFT+DMFT) are known and have not undermined the framework.
uncertainties: Theory prizes are harder to define as a discovery, and a committee may ask for a sharper physical discovery.
Remaining methodological ambiguities in DFT+DMFT (double counting, choice of correlated subspace).
Credit among Metzner, Vollhardt, Georges, Kotliar and others is open.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The Bistritzer-MacDonald flat-band prediction at the magic angle, followed by the experimental discovery of correlated insulators and superconductivity in twisted bilayer graphene, created the moiré quantum materials field. It is a rare case where theory predicted a specific condition and experiment found remarkable new correlated phases, and it is a platform for tunable quantum states.
assessment.attribution: Bistritzer and MacDonald gave the continuum model and the magic-angle prediction. Jarillo-Herrero's group made the decisive 2018 observations. Cao and Fatemi, who did much of the experimental work, are not in the credited names. A fair configuration is possible, but the theory side has two names and one could be dropped.
assessment.maturity: About eight years of intense work with independent confirmation by several groups. The mechanism of superconductivity and the nature of the correlated states are still debated, so the interpretation is not yet stable.
uncertainties: Mechanism of the superconductivity remains unresolved.
Sample dependence and twist-angle disorder complicate reproducibility.
Possible premature recognition relative to the field's maturity.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Magnetic skyrmion lattices in chiral magnets, real-space imaging, and the emergent electrodynamics they produce (topological Hall effect, spin-transfer at ultralow currents) form a clear physical discovery in magnetism with a link to spintronics. It is close to my own field and matches the interplay of theory and measurement I value.
assessment.attribution: Pfleiderer's group found the skyrmion lattice in MnSi by neutron scattering, Tokura's group imaged it in real space and extended it to other materials, and Rosch gave the theory of emergent electrodynamics and current-driven motion. The theoretical prediction by Bogdanov and coworkers predates these and is not among the credited names, which weakens a clean claim of first prediction.
assessment.maturity: Fifteen years of confirmation in many materials, including room-temperature skyrmions. Applications in racetrack memory remain unproven, but the scientific discovery is firm.
uncertainties: Priority of the theoretical prediction (Bogdanov) lies outside the credited names.
Practical impact is still prospective.
The balance between discovery and emergent-electrodynamics theory in the prize citation is unclear.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Room-temperature tunnel magnetoresistance in magnetic tunnel junctions opened the route to MRAM and to modern read heads, and the later coherent-tunnelling MgO junctions showed large effects that DFT-based theory explained through symmetry-dependent filtering. It combines a clear physical effect with large technological use, and the theory-experiment link is strong.
assessment.attribution: Miyazaki and Moodera independently reported large room-temperature TMR in 1995. Parkin's group and Yuasa and colleagues (not credited) demonstrated giant TMR in MgO junctions in 2004, with the theory by Butler and by Mathon and Umerski also outside the credited names. The three credited names are plausible but the allocation across 1995 and 2004 is disputed.
assessment.maturity: Thirty years of use in devices, so very mature. The 2007 prize for giant magnetoresistance covers a related field, so the committee may see this as an incremental follow-up.
uncertainties: Overlap with the 2007 GMR prize may reduce appetite for a spintronics award.
Credit for the MgO breakthrough involves people outside the credited names.
Whether the discovery or the engineering is the prize-worthy part.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Anyonic exchange statistics are a fundamental extension of quantum statistics beyond bosons and fermions. Direct experimental evidence in fractional quantum Hall systems, from Fabry-Perot interferometry and anyon collider experiments, turns a long-standing prediction into verified physics, and it matters for topological quantum computing.
assessment.attribution: Halperin predicted fractional statistics in the quantum Hall hierarchy, with Arovas, Schrieffer and Wilczek. Fève's collider and Manfra's interferometer experiments gave the demonstrations, and other groups (for example Nakamura and collaborators) also contributed. The theory credit for anyons is split with candidate B003 and is unresolved here.
assessment.maturity: The experiments are recent (about 2020 onward), with a few independent confirmations in graphene and GaAs. Interpretation is largely consistent but still under scrutiny, so recognition may be premature.
uncertainties: Overlap with the anyon theory candidate B003 and with Wilczek, Leinaas, Myrheim credit.
The set of experimental groups that deserve credit is larger than the three credited names.
Non-abelian statistics remain unconfirmed.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Altermagnetism identifies a third basic class of collinear magnetic order, with compensated moments but spin-split bands, and it follows from symmetry and first-principles calculations. It is a clean conceptual advance in magnetism with potential for spintronics, and the first-principles side is quantitative.
assessment.attribution: Šmejkal, Sinova and Jungwirth formulated the classification and predicted candidate materials, and earlier related work by Hayami, Yanagi and Kusunose and by Yuan and collaborators is relevant. Experimental evidence (ARPES in MnTe and CrSb, 2024) comes from other groups. The credited trio is plausible for theory but the allocation with early related predictions is not settled.
assessment.maturity: The concept dates to about 2019-2022 and experimental confirmation is recent. It is promising but young, so recognition now would be premature.
uncertainties: Few independent experiments and no major device yet.
Priority relative to earlier related theories is unresolved.
Long-term impact is uncertain.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The iron-based superconductors were the second family of high-temperature superconductors, with transition temperatures above 50 K, and gave a new setting to test theories of unconventional pairing. The discovery is clear and was verified quickly. Electronic-structure calculations played a visible role in characterising the Fermi surface and magnetism.
assessment.attribution: Hosono's group reported superconductivity in LaFeAsO1-xFx in 2008, and groups led by Chen and by Zhao rapidly raised Tc in the rare-earth analogues. Hosono is the clear originator. Whether Chen or Zhao should share the prize is open, and I would choose Hosono and Zhao on balance.
assessment.maturity: Seventeen years of independent confirmation. Tc has not risen beyond the first results in bulk and the pairing mechanism is still debated. The field has been less transformative than expected, which weighs against recognition.
uncertainties: Pairing mechanism remains unresolved.
Division of credit between Hosono, Chen and Zhao is disputed.
Scientific and practical impact may be considered smaller than for the cuprates.
